Title: Before tiny flash drives, IBM sold its original floppy disk in what size?
AnswerDetails: The original IBM floppy was eight inches across. Your pocket would have needed an upgrade!

Title: IBM began selling floppy disk drives in which year?
AnswerDetails: IBM started selling the drives in 1971. That is a lot earlier than the little disk icon many people still recognize.

Title: What fishy code name did IBM give its floppy-disk project?
AnswerDetails: The project was called Minnow. A small-fish name helped launch a very big change in data storage.

Title: Who invented the World Wide Web while working at CERN?
AnswerDetails: Tim Berners-Lee invented the Web at CERN in 1989. The idea began with helping researchers share information.

Title: The first website was about what?
AnswerDetails: The first site explained the Web project itself. A website about websites: wonderfully on brand.

Title: Which computer hosted the first website?
AnswerDetails: Berners-Lee hosted it on his NeXT computer. The Web had a surprisingly small starting address.

Title: The programming language Python got its name from what?
AnswerDetails: Guido van Rossum was reading scripts from Monty Python’s Flying Circus. The language’s name is a comedy reference, not a reptile requirement.

Title: Who created the programming language Python?
AnswerDetails: Guido van Rossum began implementing Python. His choice of name gave programmers permission to have a little fun along the way.

Title: DENSO WAVE announced the QR Code in which year?
AnswerDetails: The QR Code was announced in 1994. Those little squares were working long before restaurant menus made them dinner companions.

Title: Nintendo’s original Game Boy launched in Japan in which year?
AnswerDetails: The original Game Boy arrived in Japan in 1989. Portable gaming suddenly had a very recognizable traveling companion.

Title: What does the QR in QR Code stand for?
AnswerDetails: QR means Quick Response. Fast reading was a central goal of its design.

Title: A QR Code stores information in which directions?
AnswerDetails: QR Codes are two-dimensional codes. Their information uses both directions rather than just one.

Title: What is the job of the prominent square detection marks on a QR Code?
AnswerDetails: The square patterns help a reader find the code and its orientation. Rotating the menu is not a secret decoding ritual.
OptionB: Show the price of the item
OptionC: Help the reader locate and orient it

Title: Apple’s 2001 iPod launch promised up to how many songs in your pocket?
AnswerDetails: Apple advertised up to 1,000 songs. That was a memorable pitch for a pocket-sized music collection.

Title: What connection did the original 2001 iPod use to transfer music from a Mac?
AnswerDetails: The original iPod used FireWire. Lightning and USB-C belong to later chapters of Apple’s cable collection.

Title: What kind of storage held music inside the original 2001 iPod?
AnswerDetails: It contained a five-gigabyte hard drive. Your playlist was taking a tiny spinning-disk road trip.

Title: Bluetooth technology is named after which historical figure?
AnswerDetails: The name honors King Harald Bluetooth. The connection theme was about bringing different worlds together.

Title: Bluetooth was originally conceived as a wireless replacement for what?
AnswerDetails: Bluetooth began as a way to replace data cables with short-range wireless links. Fewer tangled wires was the mission, not free battery power.

Title: What did Sony’s original TPS-L2 Walkman play?
AnswerDetails: The TPS-L2 was a portable cassette player introduced in 1979. This playlist needed an actual tape, not a download.

Title: To estimate your position, GPS uses signals sent by what?
AnswerDetails: GPS receivers use satellite signals and their travel times. Finding the snack stop involves some very precise timing.

Title: Which web language describes the structure of a page?
AnswerDetails: HTML marks out a page’s structure. Think headings and paragraphs before choosing their party outfits.

Title: Which web technology controls colors, spacing, and visual styling?
AnswerDetails: CSS controls how web content looks. It is the wardrobe department, not the address book.

Title: What does HTTP stand for?
AnswerDetails: HTTP is the HyperText Transfer Protocol. It supplies rules for transferring web resources between systems such as browsers and servers.

Title: Compared with plain HTTP, what does HTTPS add to the connection?
AnswerDetails: HTTPS carries HTTP over a secure TLS channel. It protects the connection; it does not make every claim on a page correct.

Title: Which internet system helps translate a name like example.com into an IP address?
AnswerDetails: DNS associates domain names with resources such as IP addresses. It saves humans from memorizing a lot of numbers.

Title: A URL is most commonly known as what?
AnswerDetails: A URL tells software where a resource can be found. It is an address, not a guarantee that the destination is interesting.

Title: A website returns 404. What does that status mean?
AnswerDetails: A 404 means the server cannot find the requested resource. The page may be missing; the entire internet has not vanished.
OptionB: The requested resource was not found

Title: Which browser item can help a website remember your preferences?
AnswerDetails: A web cookie stores a small piece of information through the browser. This kind remembers preferences rather than leaving crumbs.

Title: What does a web cache keep for possible reuse?
AnswerDetails: A web cache temporarily keeps responses that may be reused under suitable conditions. Sometimes the browser can reuse the answer instead of asking again.
OptionD: A permanent copy of every website

Title: Safari, Firefox, and Chrome are examples of what?
AnswerDetails: These are programs that retrieve and display web pages. A browser is your viewing tool, not the same thing as a search engine.

Title: Which accessory was bundled with Mario Paint for the Super NES?
AnswerDetails: Mario Paint came with the Super NES Mouse. Mario traded some jumping time for pointing and painting.

Title: Which 1993 Nintendo game first used the Super FX chip?
AnswerDetails: Star Fox introduced the Super FX chip in a game. The chip helped give its space battles their distinctive polygonal look.

Title: Nintendo’s Hands Free NES controller used head movements and what for its A and B buttons?
AnswerDetails: The controller used breath input for the buttons. It offered another way to play beyond holding a conventional controller.

Title: The Game Boy Player brought Game Boy games to the television through which console?
AnswerDetails: The Game Boy Player was a GameCube accessory. Small-screen adventures got a much bigger stage.

Title: What physical format did the original PlayStation primarily use for its games?
AnswerDetails: PlayStation used CD-ROM games. The format supported larger games than contemporary cartridge alternatives.

Title: Where did original PlayStation players commonly save game progress?
AnswerDetails: Players used separate memory cards. Remembering your save could be almost as important as remembering the game.

Title: How many little squares make up a standard Tetris piece?
AnswerDetails: Each piece consists of four connected squares. Four blocks, endless decisions about where to put them.

Title: How many distinct standard piece shapes are used in classic Tetris?
AnswerDetails: Classic Tetris uses seven shapes. Such a small cast can cause an impressive amount of last-second panic.

Title: What was the Nintendo DS’s standout screen arrangement?
AnswerDetails: The DS combined two screens with touch input. A second view could stay visible instead of replacing the first.

Title: In Minecraft, which material acts like wiring to carry power and signals?
AnswerDetails: Redstone dust transmits power and signals between components. Minecraft builders can give their creations more than good looks.

Title: A Boolean value has which two possible states?
AnswerDetails: A Boolean is either true or false. Computers use those crisp choices even when humans prefer “maybe.”

Title: Which everyday object is a useful example of an algorithm?
AnswerDetails: An algorithm is a series of instructions for carrying out a task. A recipe counts, even before anyone adds a computer.

Title: Which kind of compression lets you reconstruct the original data exactly?
AnswerDetails: Lossless compression preserves enough information to recover the exact original. Smaller packaging, nothing thrown away.

Title: What can lossy compression do to make a file smaller?
AnswerDetails: Lossy methods discard some information. The trade-off is a smaller file rather than an exact round trip.

Title: What is a basic building block of a digital display called?
AnswerDetails: A pixel is a basic display building block. Lots of these tiny elements work together to make the picture.

Title: A display described as 800 × 600 pixels is how many pixels wide?
AnswerDetails: The first number gives the width; the second gives the height. Here that is 800 pixels across and 600 down.

Title: Which programming feature is designed to repeat a sequence of instructions?
AnswerDetails: A loop repeats instructions according to its rules. It is how code says “do that again” without typing the same command endlessly.

Title: What do programmers call values supplied as inputs when calling a function?
AnswerDetails: Arguments are inputs passed into a function. In programming, having arguments can be entirely productive.

Title: Which structure stores an ordered collection of items, such as a list of player names?
AnswerDetails: An array stores an ordered collection. Its items can be reached by their indexes rather than by shouting for them.

Title: In a JavaScript array, what index identifies the first item?
AnswerDetails: JavaScript array indexes start at zero. The first player gets position zero without coming in last.

Title: Training on photos paired with correct labels such as “cat” and “dog” is an example of what?
AnswerDetails: Supervised learning uses examples with known answers. The labels give the model a target to learn from.

Title: A model sorts emails into “spam” or “not spam.” What kind of task is this?
AnswerDetails: Classification predicts membership in categories. Here there are two possible categories, so it is binary classification.

Title: A model predicts tomorrow’s temperature as a number. What kind of task is this?
AnswerDetails: Regression predicts numerical values. This model is estimating a quantity rather than picking a category.

Title: Grouping unlabeled music tracks by similarities is an example of what?
AnswerDetails: Clustering organizes similar items into groups. It can find groupings without being handed a label for every example.

Title: In machine learning, an embedding represents an item as what?
AnswerDetails: An embedding represents data with a vector. Numbers let a model work with relationships between items mathematically.

Title: In a useful embedding space, similar items are generally placed how?
AnswerDetails: Nearby positions can encode similarity. The coordinates are learned representations, not a literal map of where objects live.

Title: A model aces its training examples but struggles on new ones. What problem might it have?
AnswerDetails: Overfitting means fitting the training data too closely to work well on new cases. Memorizing the practice sheet is not the same as mastering the topic.

Title: In a language model, a text token can be which of these?
AnswerDetails: Tokens are units of text processing, and their sizes vary. A long word does not automatically get a single VIP token.
OptionD: A word, part of a word, or character

Title: What does a language model estimate when considering possible text continuations?
AnswerDetails: Language models estimate probabilities for text sequences. Likely wording is not the same thing as verified truth.
OptionB: The physical weight of each word
OptionC: Probabilities of tokens or token sequences
OptionD: A guarantee that each claim is true

Title: Which algorithm is central to training neural networks by working backward through prediction errors?
AnswerDetails: Backpropagation calculates how a neural network’s error changes with its weights, helping an optimizer adjust them. Working backward helps the next prediction move forward!
